findings.summary: ARM AArch32 is a 32-bit RISC instruction set architecture introduced in 1985, forming the foundation of ARM's embedded and mobile processor designs. It defines a register file of 15 general-purpose 32-bit registers plus a link register, with the program counter separate. The architecture supports two instruction encodings: the fixed 32-bit ARM mode and the mixed 16/32-bit Thumb-2 mode for improved code density. Extensions include Jazelle for Java bytecode handling, various DSP and cryptography extensions, and floating-point units. AArch32 operates in a bi-endian mode with little-endian as default. The architecture has evolved through versions ARMv7-M, ARMv7-R, ARMv7-A, and ARMv8-M/R, maintaining backward compatibility while adding features. It serves as the 32-bit complement to the 64-bit AArch64, sharing the same architectural roots but with distinct encoding and register conventions.

mechanisms.title: Register File and PC Separation
mechanisms.explanation: AArch32 provides 15 × 32-bit general-purpose registers (R0-R14) plus a dedicated link register (R14) and a separate program counter (R15). This design supports subroutine calls through the link register and position-independent code. The 26-bit program counter in older versions limited address space to 64 MB, later expanded to 32-bit in ARMv3 and beyond.

mechanisms.title: Dual Encoding Modes
mechanisms.explanation: AArch32 supports two instruction encodings: the standard 32-bit ARM mode and the Thumb-2 mode which mixes 16-bit and 32-bit instructions. This dual-mode approach improves code density while maintaining performance, with the processor switching between modes using branch-and-link instructions or state-bit manipulation in the program counter.
